547.title: Not one sparrow (Luke 12:1–12)
547.hook: five sparrows sold for two pennies, and none forgotten; your hairs are numbered
547.howItsDone: The hymn His Eye Is on the Sparrow draws on the sparrow sayings in Matthew and Luke, and Francis of Assisi is remembered for preaching to the birds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, alms: a cup made clean from the inside out, and your line, the inside too.

Luke says the crowd had grown past counting, so big that people were treading on one another. And Jesus turns first to his own friends and talks about fear. Theirs: fear of being found out, fear of powerful people, fear of standing before judges one day and not knowing what to say. It's a heavy start. Then, to make his point, he reaches for something small from the marketplace: sparrows, sold five at a time.

In the King James Bible: "Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings, and not one of them is forgotten before God?" Farthing is the King James word for a small coin; the Greek says assarion. Now set Luke beside Matthew. In Matthew, two sparrows are sold for one farthing. In Luke, five for two. Some readers do the arithmetic: pay for four, and the seller throws in a fifth for free, a bird not even worth a price. And not one of them, Jesus says, is forgotten before God. Then he comes closer: "But even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows." Numbered. Not loved in general, as a crowd, but known down to a detail you don't even know about yourself. That's the ground under everything else he says here. Don't fear those who can only kill the body. Say openly who you belong to. And when you're dragged before authorities, don't rehearse a speech, because, as he puts it, "the Holy Ghost shall teach you in the same hour what ye ought to say." In Acts, Luke's second book, Peter and Paul do stand before councils and governors. Courage, in this passage, doesn't come from being tough. It comes from being known: if not one sparrow is forgotten, Jesus tells his friends, they need not fear.
screen: then, large: `NOT ONE OF THEM IS FORGOTTEN BEFORE GOD.`

segments.voice: Think of the thing you're most afraid of this week, and hold it for a moment. Then picture the fifth sparrow, the one thrown in for free, and the line that not one of them is forgotten. If you pray, place your fear next to that sparrow; if you don't, simply hold the fear and the sparrow side by side.
Assarion, the small Greek coin sparrows were sold for: five birds for two coins, the fifth one thrown in free, and not one of them forgotten before God.
Your line: not one forgotten. Even the hairs of your head are numbered. See you tomorrow.

548.title: Rich toward God (Luke 12:13–21)
548.hook: someone asks him to split an inheritance, and he warns against greed
548.howItsDone: Christians read the rich fool when thinking about money, wills and generosity; some churches teach tithing, giving a set share of income, and some Christians name charities in their wills as a way of being rich toward God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, assarion: five sparrows for two small coins, and your line, not one forgotten.

Jesus has just been talking about courage before judges and the Holy Spirit's help, and a voice from the crowd cuts right across it: "Master, speak to my brother, that he divide the inheritance with me." You can almost hear the family behind it. A parent has died. Someone thinks they got less than their share. There have been arguments at the kitchen table, and maybe nobody's speaking now. So the man brings it to the teacher everyone is listening to. Surely he'll take my side.

The law of Moses had rules for how an inheritance was split, but Jesus won't do it: "Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?" He goes underneath the question: "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth." The Greek word for covetousness is pleonexia, the itch for more. Not wanting things, exactly; wanting more than. More than my brother. More than last year. Then a story. A rich man's land produces a huge harvest, and he has a conversation. Listen to who's in it. He thinks within himself. I will pull down my barns, I will build greater. Then he talks to his own soul: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry." No family, no neighbor, no worker who brought the harvest in, no God. Only him, his barns and his soul. That night, God speaks for the first time in the story and calls him a fool. His life is required of him, and who will own it all now? Then the last line: "So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God." Rich toward God. Not poor, necessarily. Rich in a direction: wealth that faces outward, toward God and other people, instead of inward into bigger barns. And it loops back to the brothers. An inheritance fight is exactly what the rich fool's barns could turn into.

Bring to mind a small disagreement you're carrying: whose turn it is to do the dishes, who owes whom for lunch, a borrowed thing never returned, a sibling squabble about something left behind. Notice the part of you that keeps score, then imagine letting the score go, giving a little more than your share, and ask what that would really cost you. If you pray, ask for a heart that faces outward.
Pleonexia, Greek for covetousness, the itch for more: wealth that faces outward, toward God and other people, instead of inward into bigger barns and a conversation with only yourself.
Your line: treasure that faces outward. Rich, but in a direction. Day five hundred forty-eight.

549.title: Fear not, little flock (Luke 12:22–34)
549.hook: it's your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom
549.howItsDone: Some Christians return to this passage in times of money worry, and some religious communities, such as Franciscan friars and Poor Clares, give up personal possessions as a discipline of trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pleonexia, the itch for more, and a rich man who talked only to his soul. Your line was treasure that faces outward.

This time the words are for his disciples, not the crowd. Fishermen who left their boats. A former tax collector. Women supporting the group out of their own means. No house of their own, no regular income, heading toward Jerusalem with a teacher who keeps making powerful people angry. If anyone had reason to lie awake doing sums, it was this group. And he looks at them, a small band on a dusty road, and calls them by a tender name.
screen: `A SMALL BAND ON A DUSTY ROAD.`

segments.voice: First he points at the sky: "Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap; which neither have storehouse nor barn; and God feedeth them." Matthew just says the birds. Luke names ravens, scavengers, a bird the law of Moses listed as unclean. Even the bird nobody would put on a greeting card is fed. Then the field: "Consider the lilies how they grow: they toil not, they spin not; and yet I say unto you, that Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these." Then a sharp little question: which of you, by worrying, can add one cubit to your height, or a single hour to your life? And the line Luke saves for last: "Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom." Little flock: small, vulnerable, the kind of group a wolf would notice. He doesn't pretend they're strong. He says they're loved. Good pleasure is a warm phrase in Greek, from the same family as the angels' good will toward men at his birth, and the voice at his baptism: in thee I am well pleased. In Jesus' words, the kingdom isn't handed over reluctantly, after enough worry. It's the Father's delight to give it. Then: sell what you have, give alms, keep treasure where moths and thieves can't reach. The giving follows the not fearing. And the line that sums up the chapter so far: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."

Let one worry about money or the future come up and name it plainly, then think of the ravens, fed without a barn, and let it sit a little lighter. Think of one thing you could give away, a coat you don't wear, a book you've finished, something you'd notice but not miss terribly, and picture handing it over. If you pray, say the line quietly: fed without a barn.
Fear not. Jesus' words to a small, vulnerable band of followers: it is your Father's good pleasure, God's delight, to give you the kingdom.
Your line: fed without a barn. Ravens keep no storehouse, and they're fed. That's day five hundred forty-nine.

550.title: Lamps burning (Luke 12:35–59)
550.hook: be like servants waiting up for their master
550.howItsDone: Christians read watching passages like this one especially in Advent, the season of waiting before Christmas, and many churches keep a candle burning or light a new one each week as a sign of readiness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ravens, lilies, and a little flock told fear not. Your line was fed without a barn.

A big house, late at night. The master has gone to a wedding feast, and in that world a wedding could run for days, so nobody knows when he'll be back. Midnight? Three in the morning? The servants could all go to bed. Or they could do what Jesus describes: keep their robes tucked into their belts, the oil lamps trimmed and burning, and listen for a knock. Anyone who has waited up for a teenager, or sat by the phone for news from a hospital, knows this kind of night.

In the King James Bible: "Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning." People wore long robes, and to run or work you tucked the hem up into your belt. It's the ancient way of saying roll up your sleeves. Then the most surprising sentence in the passage: "Blessed are those servants, whom the lord when he cometh shall find watching: verily I say unto you, that he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them." The master comes home at midnight, finds his servants awake, and instead of being served, he ties on an apron and serves them dinner. Everything upside down. Christians hear in it the same Jesus who, in John's Gospel, washes his friends' feet. What are they waiting for? Most Christians read this as the return of Christ at the end of time, which, Jesus says, comes at an hour when you think not. Many also hear it about every ordinary day: being awake to God, and to people, right now. The chapter grows more urgent. "For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required." You can read the sky and know rain is coming, Jesus says, so why can't you read this moment? And if you have a quarrel, settle it on the way, before it reaches the judge. All of it says one thing. Don't sleepwalk. The knock could come in the middle of any conversation.

Be like a servant listening for a knock: notice every sound, a car, a clock, your own breath, and when your mind drifts, bring it back the way you'd jolt upright at footsteps by the door. Then think of one conversation you usually half listen to, and picture yourself fully awake in it, phone down, eyes up, really hearing. If you pray, ask to be found watching.
Lamps burning. Servants waiting up with their robes tucked in and their lights lit, and a master who comes home and serves them.
Your line: keep your lamps lit. In this story, the master comes home and serves. Day five hundred fifty, done.

551.title: One more year (Luke 13:1–9)
551.hook: a barren fig tree gets one more year of digging and manure
551.howItsDone: In the Catholic Sunday readings, Luke 13:1–9 falls in Lent, the season of repentance, and some Christians hear the gardener as Christ pleading for time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lamps burning, and a master who came home and served his servants. Your line was keep your lamps lit.

The news comes first. Some people tell Jesus that Pilate, the Roman governor, has killed Galileans while they were offering sacrifices. Jesus adds another disaster: a tower at Siloam, in Jerusalem, collapsed and killed eighteen people. When disaster strikes, someone says it out loud, or thinks it quietly: they must have done something. Jesus asks it directly. Were they worse than everyone else? "I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish." Then, instead of explaining suffering, he tells a story about a tree.

A man has a fig tree planted in his vineyard. Three years running he comes looking for fruit and finds none. So he tells the gardener, in the King James Bible: "cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?" It's a fair question. The tree has taken up ground for three years and given nothing back. But the gardener answers: "Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it." Dung it. Manure. He doesn't just ask for more time; he offers to get his hands dirty, loosening the hard ground round the roots and feeding it with the least glamorous stuff on the farm. A small thing in the Greek is worth knowing. Let it alone is a form of aphiēmi, the ordinary verb for let go, leave be. It's also the word the Gospels use for forgive, as in forgive us our sins. So to a Greek ear the request sounds a little like a plea for mercy. Some Christian readers hear Jesus himself in the gardener, pleading for time and doing the digging. Then the story stops: if it bears fruit, well; if not, cut it down after that. We never find out what happened next year. Luke leaves the ending open, the way a life is open. It's a story about urgency, the year is real and it ends, and about patience, the kind that works the soil instead of just waiting. Disaster doesn't prove anyone deserved it; and the year the gardener asks for is a year of digging.
screen: then, large: `LET IT ALONE THIS YEAR ALSO.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've been close to writing off, a colleague who never delivers, a relative who keeps letting you down, or maybe yourself, and picture them as the fig tree and yourself as the gardener asking for one more season. What would digging around the roots look like: a real conversation, some help, a little patience with a deadline? If you pray, ask for the gardener's patience.
Aphiēmi, the Greek verb for let it alone, leave be — the gardener's plea for a fruitless fig tree he offers to dig and feed, while the story never tells us how it turned out.
Your line: leave it one more year. Patience, in this story, gets its hands dirty. See you tomorrow.

552.title: The bent-over woman (Luke 13:10–17)
552.hook: eighteen years stooped; he calls her a daughter of Abraham and she stands up straight
552.howItsDone: Some churches pray for the sick with the laying on of hands, as Jesus does here, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians also anoint the sick with oil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, aphiēmi, let it alone: a gardener's plea for a fig tree, and your line, leave it one more year.

Eighteen years. That is how long, Luke says, this woman has been bent over, looking at the ground: feet, dust, the hems of other people's clothes. She can't look up to see a face or the sky. Luke, who tradition says was a physician, describes her carefully: she "was bowed together, and could in no wise lift up herself." On a Sabbath she does what she has probably done for years. She comes to the synagogue. Nobody says she asked for anything. Jesus is teaching, and he sees her.

He calls her over: "Woman, thou art loosed from thine infirmity." He lays his hands on her, "and immediately she was made straight, and glorified God." After eighteen years, perhaps the first thing she sees, looking up, is his face. Then comes an objection worth hearing fairly. The leader of the synagogue is indignant and tells the crowd: "There are six days in which men ought to work: in them therefore come and be healed, and not on the sabbath day." He's protecting something precious, the Sabbath rest God commanded. He isn't against healing; he's against doing it today. Jesus answers with an argument the leader would recognize, from the lesser to the greater. On the Sabbath, every one of you unties your ox or donkey and leads it to water. Then: "And ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan hath bound, lo, these eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the sabbath day?" In Luke's Greek, untie and loose are the same verb, and bound is its opposite. If an animal can be untied for a drink, how much more a woman bound for eighteen years? And notice the title: daughter of Abraham. For eighteen years she had been the bent woman, a body people stepped around. He gives her a family name, a place in Israel's story. Luke says all the people rejoiced. The Sabbath, a day of freedom, became the day she was set free.
screen: then, large: `SHE WAS MADE STRAIGHT, AND GLORIFIED GOD.`

segments.voice: Stand if you can, or sit forward, and let your head drop toward your chest; notice how small the world gets. Then roll slowly upward, one bone at a time, until your eyes find the room, and breathe at your full height, thinking of whatever has kept you bent lately: a weight, a worry, someone's words. If you pray, hear the words thou art loosed; if you don't, simply stand in your own height.
Abraham. Jesus calls the bent-over woman a daughter of Abraham as he heals her, giving her a family name and a place in Israel's story.
Your line: daughter, you are loosed. Eighteen years ended with a touch. Day five hundred fifty-two.

553.title: Like a mother hen (Luke 13:18–35)
553.hook: how often I would have gathered you, as a hen gathers her chicks
553.howItsDone: Some churches read Jesus' lament over Jerusalem in Lent, and on the Mount of Olives, the chapel of Dominus Flevit has a mosaic of a hen gathering her chicks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a bent-over woman stood straight and was called a daughter of Abraham. Your line was daughter, you are loosed.

A warning arrives on the road. Some Pharisees come to Jesus, and it seems they're trying to help: "Get thee out, and depart hence: for Herod will kill thee." Herod, the ruler of Galilee, the man who, Luke has told us, beheaded John the Baptist. This is a real threat. Jesus sends back a message with a bite in it: "Go ye, and tell that fox" that I'm busy healing today and tomorrow, and on the third day I'll finish. A fox. Hold onto that animal, because a few sentences later Jesus picks an animal for himself.

He doesn't choose a lion, or an eagle. He looks toward Jerusalem, the city he's heading for, and says, in the King James Bible: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee; how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings, and ye would not!" A hen, an ordinary farmyard bird. When danger comes, a hawk overhead, a fox at the fence, she can't fight it off. What she can do is spread her wings, call her chicks, and put her own body between them and harm. So: Herod the fox, and Jesus the mother hen. One hunts. The other covers, even at a cost. The image wasn't new. Israel's psalms had long pictured God's protection as wings. Psalm 91: "He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust." Jesus makes that old picture a mother's. And the lament is full of grief, not anger: how often I would have, and you would not. Love that can be refused. The rest of the passage has the same open arms: people will come from east and west, north and south, and sit down in the kingdom of God; and some who are last will be first. Then the week behind us: a sparrow not forgotten, a barn too big, a little flock, lamps burning, a tree given one more year, a bent woman standing straight, and now a hen with her wings open, over a city that might not come.
